title: Choose the visual world for dollarvote
question: The roll assigned The Tally Board. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Tally Board
options.lineage: the electronic vote display boards on the House chamber walls, as seen on C-SPAN
options.thesis: Every legislator is a lamp on the chamber board, and your 5 interests decide which lamps light up.
materials: yea/nay lamp cells with Y and N letters
options.viewport: Your 5 picks sit across the top as lit selector keys. Below, the full board of 535 name strips re-sorts in place, and the best-aligned members burn brightest.
options.risk: Green and red lamps read as pass and fail, so every lamp also carries a letter and a number, and the axis categories need their direction stated in words.

raised.raise: The board keeps a fixed cell grid. Changing a pick re-sorts the rows in place with a per-cell cascade, and columns never move.
Rows keep their identity while they re-rank, and a row that moved stays marked until the visitor has seen it.
Each of your 5 interests owns one lamp color on every screen: the board, the legislator page and the bill page.
Inside the board, rank shows through weight, case and reversed cells, not bigger type.

options.label: The Sample Ballot
options.lineage: the paper sample ballot mailed before every election
options.thesis: You mark 5 ovals, and the ballot hands back the legislators who voted your way.
options.viewport: A ballot sheet with 24 interests as ovals in contest columns. Marking the fifth one turns the sheet into a ranked results column.
options.risk: It's the most familiar civic metaphor, and the ballot can read as an actual election ballot.

options.label: Boarding Pass & Gate Board
options.lineage: airline boarding passes and live gate boards
options.thesis: Your 5 interests print on a pass, and the board re-ranks every legislator against it.
options.viewport: A segmented pass holds your 5 picks on the left. On the right, a ranked board reorders rows in place.
options.case: It's very clear about ranking, but visitors connect less with air travel than with the chamber board.
options.risk: The travel metaphor has nothing to do with Congress, so it can feel like a costume.

options.label: Split-Flap Concourse
options.thesis: Legislators clatter into rank on a departure board.
options.viewport: A full-width flap board of ranked names.
options.case: It's the same family as the chamber board, but without any tie to Congress.
options.risk: The flapping becomes a gimmick after the first sort.
options.kept: Fixed cell grid; only the cells change.

options.label: Midnight Transit Diagram
options.thesis: Interests are lines, and legislators are stations where they cross.
options.viewport: Five colored lines across a city of names.
options.case: The metaphor fights the ranking job, and visitors don't think of their interests as routes.
options.kept: Each chosen line keeps its color everywhere.

options.label: Timetable Slide Rack
options.thesis: One type size, with rank carried by weight and reversal.
options.case: Sideways travel through slides hides a ranking a visitor needs to see all at once.
options.risk: Slanted containers fight a dense table.
options.kept: Rank by weight, case and reversal, not size.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean civic-data dashboard: checkbox filters on the left, a sortable legislator table, and party-colored badges.
canonCard.viewport: Filters on the left, ranked table on the right.
canonCard.risk: It looks like every civic-tech site, and the party colors pull attention away from interests.
